sources.name: The Guardian
sources.summary: Soho theatre, London The standup throws himself into ‘13 or 14 pieces of humour’ that confirm his gifts for escalating everyday apercus into absurd delights Paul Foot made quite the impression with 2023’s Dissolve , a mid-career breakout from his oddball groove. The Future confirms the 52-year-old as a comic any audience could enjoy, and – to some degree – develops his newfound interest in the real world and the circumstances of his own life. Not that it begins with any seriousness of purpose, as our host throws himself into a series of escalating set pieces built on everyday apercus – how reassuring we find it, say, when a Chinese restaurant is frequented by Chinese diners. Then comes the swerve, which is less well integrated, and less remarkable, than in the show’s predecessor, but affecting nonetheless. Before that, the first half is all about Foot’s free-standing bits (“about 13 or 14 pieces of humour”, he calls them): concentrated bursts of observational comedy, in which he inflates a workaday premise to absurdity and beyond. The etiquette of British funerals; over-excitement at food served on sizzling hot-plates – Foot constructing teetering towers of nonsense from it all with a voice and range of facial expression evoking British comedy at its ooh-missus, nudge-nudge heyday.
